name: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
title: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
answer: Board advisory and fiduciary risk covers the duties directors owe when a company adopts or relies on artificial intelligence. It includes oversight of AI strategy, risk appetite, internal controls, and public disclosures about AI use. The work sits at the intersection of corporate law, securities regulation, and emerging AI governance expectations. Directors face questions about whether AI systems are used in ways that could harm the company, its customers, or its shareholders.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This practice runs on board portals, enterprise risk registers, and compliance libraries that track AI-specific regulation. Many boards use AI governance platforms to log model inventories, risk ratings, and audit trails. The underlying reference material includes corporate charters, committee mandates, and the regulatory pages that map state and federal AI requirements.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through board education sessions, AI risk assessments, and periodic reviews of model use cases against fiduciary duties. Legal counsel and compliance officers prepare briefings that translate technical AI risks into board-level questions about oversight, disclosure, and internal controls. Audit and risk committees typically receive standing updates on AI incidents, model changes, and regulatory developments.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area center on the board's duty of oversight and the risk of personal liability for failing to monitor AI-related harms. Provenance matters because directors must be able to show that they relied on competent experts, reviewed material information, and documented their decision-making. Fiduciary risk also includes conflicts of interest where AI vendors, data sources, or board members have competing interests.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Board advisory and fiduciary risk is moving toward more explicit regulatory expectations for AI oversight and director competence. Courts and regulators are beginning to test whether traditional fiduciary duties extend to AI-specific harms such as biased decisions, privacy breaches, and model failures. The trend is toward standing board committees with AI expertise, more granular disclosure of AI risk, and closer scrutiny of board minutes and audit trails.
